title: Performance evidence ops handbook
body:
Purpose:
This is an operational handbook for assembling defensible performance + unit-economics claims to use in sales collateral, partner briefings, and website claims. Focus: attribution (what specifically makes us faster/cheaper), repeatable experiments, scripts for field validation, and short customer-facing proof fragments.

Audience:
- GTM reps and solution engineers needing bite-sized evidence
- Product marketing drafting one-pagers and battlecards
- Field engineers running quick customer validations

Principles for any claim:
1) Headline claim: short, quantifiable statement the buyer can test in minutes. Example: "Redwood reduces per-request median generation latency by 3–5x vs competitor baseline under identical model size and sequence length."
2) Attribution line: which subsystem yields the improvement (examples: continuous batching that preserves 95th p99 cost, KV prefix caching, lower kernel overhead due to compilation choices, smarter routing to quantized instances).
3) Proof recipe: minimal benchmark description (input size, batch policy, hardware, model version, sample size, metric definitions).
4) Customer impact: convert performance delta into an economics/ROI statement (tokens/hour, $/million tokens, revenue or conversion lift).

Claim hierarchy (how to package):
- Level A (Public claim): headline + single benchmark snapshot + plain language attribution + link to deeper lab data.
- Level B (Sales-ready): Headline + 2-3 benchmark scenarios tailored to buyer archetype + short ROI example + one-sentence competitor comparator.
- Level C (Technical appendix): Raw logs, scripts, provisioning configs, and p95/p99 traces with noise analysis.

Minimum benchmark template (use for every experiment):
- Scenario name: e.g., "chat-short-2-turns-512ctx"
- Model family: e.g., llm-openx-7b-quant
- Endpoint config: batch_max=64, batch_timeout_ms=8, kv_cache=true, quantize=4bit
- Hardware: a100-40gb (or dedicated pool SKU id)
- Workload profile: 10k requests, seq_in=64, seq_out=256, concurrency ramp to steady state at 200 rps
- Metrics to collect: median latency (ms/token), p95 latency (ms), throughput (tokens/sec), gpu_util, cost per 1M tokens (in USD), error rate
- Repeats: N=5 runs, report mean and 95% bootstrap CI

Sample benchmark fragment (example data, for illustration only):
Scenario | median ms/token | p95 ms | tokens/sec | $/M tokens
chat-short-512 | 12 ms/token | 48 ms | 4200 | $18.50
chat-long-8k | 18 ms/token | 120 ms | 3200 | $22.10
batch-heavy | 9 ms/token | 60 ms | 5800 | $14.00
(Include raw CSV from harness in Level C appendix)

Attribution checklist (quick booleans to validate claim provenance):
- Did we control for model weights and quantization between comparison targets? (yes/no)
- Was routing identical (same region and network path)? (yes/no)
- Were batching policies equivalent or intentionally tuned? (document values)
- Are KV/prefix caches warm at test start? (warm/cold)

Competitive notes (operational slant):
- Competitor A (cloudLM-basic): often shows competitive median latency on single-request tests but degrades quickly under batching and KV-heavy workloads. Use: show our steady-state throughput and p95 advantage rather than single-request numbers.
- Competitor B (vendorServeX): claims cheaper per-token cost using aggressive quantization but lacks prefix/KV cache integration; highlight how our cache + routing yields lower effective cost for session-based experiences.
- GTM implication: Avoid head-to-head microbenchmarks that favor their niche; instead pick scenarios where architecture differences (caching, routing, kernel optimizations) compound advantage.

Field test playbook (30–90 minute on-customer validation):
1) Pre-call: ask for a sandbox API key or a small sample of production traffic (anonymized).
2) Run three simple scenarios: short chat (2 turns), multi-turn session (5 turns), long generation (>=2k tokens). Use the Minimum benchmark template.
3) Collect: median, p95, tokens/sec, and cost projection. Document differences as absolute deltas and percent.
4) Convert to customer math: e.g., "For your 100M tokens/mo workload, this delta maps to ~$X savings/mo and expected 0.2% lift in page load -> estimated +Y visits/mo".
5) Output: one slide with 3 charts (latency distributions, throughput curve, cost projection) and an action recommendation (PoC, migrate, or deeper evaluation).

Messaging scripts (tight bites for reps):
- Elevator (40–60 words): "We help teams run large language models with production predictability — often cutting per-token latency and effective token cost by multiples through a combination of runtime batching, prefix caching, and dynamic routing to optimized quantized variants. That means faster features and lower cost per monthly active user."
- Objection handling: "We’re faster only on certain workloads": "Good question — that’s why we run the three quick scenarios above. Most customers see the largest wins on session-based chat and high-volume embedding pipelines where caching and batching amortize fixed kernel overhead."

ROI worked example (copyable table):
Inputs: monthly tokens = 100,000,000; current cost = $30/M tokens; current p95 latency = 300 ms
Redwood projected: $18/M tokens (40% cost reduction), p95 = 80 ms (3.75x improvement)
Result: monthly cost delta = (30 - 18) * 100 = $1,200 savings; latency improvement -> estimated 5% increase in conversion for latency-sensitive flows -> revenue impact = depends on customer ARPU, illustrate with their numbers.

Proof-point prioritization for collateral (which evidence to include where):
- Website headline: single Level A claim + very high-level attribution line.
- Sales one-pager: Level B set for 2 buyer archetypes (product/ops) + ROI snippet.
- Whitepaper/tech note: Level C full rig with scripts, raw output, and noise analysis.

Guardrails for public claims:
- Never publish a public claim without: (a) competitor name redacted or with explicit consent (legal check), (b) an attached lab appendix with raw data and test configs, and (c) sign-off from eng/research owner.

Repository and automation pointers (how to make this repeatable):
- Use eval-harness repo (linked artifact) as canonical runner.
- Store all CSV outputs to the shared S3 bucket: s3://redwood-performance-evidence/[project]/[scenario]/run-YYYYMMDD.csv (ops-only).
- Tag PRs that introduce new public claims with the label: claim-evidence-required.

Quick experiments we should run next (priority list):
1) Session-warm vs session-cold economics: quantify savings from KV prefix caching across realistic session lengths for a sample of 5 customers.
2) Batching vs latency SLO envelope: find the sweet spot batch_timeout_ms across 3 model families and publish recommended defaults.
3) Routing to quantized variants: measure quality delta (BLEU/ROUGE/sampling metrics relevant to use case) and effective $/M tokens after fallback penalties.

Appendix: short checklist for publishing a Level A claim
- [ ] Experiment run N>=3, mean + CI included
- [ ] Configs attached (batching, hw, model, kv warm/cold)
- [ ] Comparison target defined & controlled for model weights/floatness
- [ ] SRE signoff on measurement validity
- [ ] Legal review if competitor named

Notes and open questions (work-in-progress):
- Need an internal standard for how we compute $/M tokens (include infra amortization, licensing, and network egress?)
- How to present quality vs cost tradeoffs consistently across model families (quantified metric basket needed)
- Request: PMs/Research add 3 canonical scenarios per product vertical (search, chat-asst, summarization) for evergreen baseline runs.

Contact for help: Ethan Carter (go-to-market), priya.nair@redwood.company for field-test coordination, eng contact: Marco Diaz.

End of handbook (working draft).
